title: Acts 10:24–48
context: Cornelius has gathered relatives and friends to hear Peter. Peter explains that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean, and Cornelius recounts his vision. Peter declares that God shows no partiality and that in every nation whoever fears him is acceptable. He proclaims Jesus, anointed with the Spirit, crucified, raised, and appointed judge, through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on the Gentile hearers, who speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter orders them baptized.

verses.text: On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.
verses.arminianNotes: Cornelius has gathered his relatives and close friends. Arminian readers see a man eager to share what God is doing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a household gathered to receive the word.

verses.text: When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him.
verses.arminianNotes: Cornelius falls at Peter’s feet in worship. Arminian commentators see sincere but misplaced reverence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see the need to direct worship to God alone.

verses.text: But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Stand up! I myself am also a man.” Arminian readers see humility in Peter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boundary between creature and Creator.

verses.text: As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter finds many people gathered. Arminian expositors see a larger audience than expected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God assembling hearers.

verses.text: He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter says God has shown him not to call any person unclean. Arminian readers see the vision interpreted as about people, not only food.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the dividing wall of Ephesians 2:14 coming down.

verses.text: Therefore I also came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”
verses.arminianNotes: He came without objection and asks why he was called. Arminian commentators see obedience overcoming reluctance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see Peter following God’s lead.

verses.text: Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing
verses.arminianNotes: Cornelius recounts his vision four days earlier. Arminian readers see his testimony matching Peter’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see two visions coordinated by one God.

verses.text: and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God.
verses.arminianNotes: His prayer was heard and his alms remembered. Arminian expositors see God valuing his seeking heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God remembering the work he began in Cornelius.

verses.text: Send therefore to Joppa and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He is staying in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’
verses.arminianNotes: He was told to send for Peter. Arminian readers see the message he needs coming through a person.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God binding salvation to the hearing of the gospel.

verses.text: Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”
verses.arminianNotes: They are all present before God to hear what the Lord commanded. Arminian commentators see a ready audience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see a congregation gathered before God, not merely before a preacher.

verses.text: Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism;
verses.arminianNotes: God shows no partiality. Arminian readers see God’s impartial love for all people, without favoritism toward any group.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see impartiality regarding nationality and status, which they hold is fully consistent with God’s free election of individuals.

verses.text: but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.
verses.arminianNotes: In every nation whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. Arminian expositors see God receiving any person who responds to the light they have.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors read this as acceptable for hearing the gospel, since Cornelius still needed Christ to be saved (11:14).

verses.text: The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all—
verses.arminianNotes: God sent the word of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all. Arminian readers see peace offered universally.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s lordship over Jew and Gentile alike.

verses.text: you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached;
verses.arminianNotes: They know what happened throughout Judea after John’s baptism. Arminian commentators see Peter starting from shared knowledge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see the gospel rooted in public history.

verses.text: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
verses.arminianNotes: God anointed Jesus with the Spirit and power, and he healed those oppressed by the devil. Arminian readers see Jesus’ compassion for the afflicted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Father anointing the Son by the Spirit for his messianic work.

verses.text: We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree.
verses.arminianNotes: The apostles witnessed his deeds, and they killed him by hanging him on a tree. Arminian expositors see testimony grounded in what they saw.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the curse of the law borne by Christ.

verses.text: God raised him up the third day and gave him to be revealed,
verses.arminianNotes: God raised him on the third day and made him appear. Arminian readers see the resurrection as the heart of the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Father vindicating the Son.

verses.text: not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
verses.arminianNotes: He appeared not to all people but to witnesses chosen beforehand by God. Arminian commentators see God selecting witnesses for a specific role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators note the phrase “chosen before by God” and see God’s sovereign selection at work in revelation.

verses.text: He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead.
verses.arminianNotes: He commanded them to testify that Jesus is appointed judge of living and dead. Arminian readers see accountability that makes the offer urgent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ appointed by God to judge, a sign of his authority.

verses.text: All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”
verses.arminianNotes: Everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Arminian expositors see the universal promise: everyone who believes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors fully affirm the promise and see faith as the God-given means of receiving forgiveness.

verses.text: While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word.
verses.arminianNotes: While Peter is still speaking, the Spirit falls on all who hear. Arminian readers see hearing and believing met immediately by God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God acting before anyone could lay on hands or administer baptism, showing salvation is his work.

verses.text: They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jewish believers are amazed that the Gentiles receive the gift. Arminian commentators see prejudice confronted by God’s action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s grace overriding human expectations.

verses.text: For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered,
verses.arminianNotes: They hear them speaking in tongues and praising God. Arminian readers see the same sign as Pentecost given to Gentiles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a Gentile Pentecost marking their full inclusion.

verses.text: “Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Who can forbid water for baptism to those who have received the Spirit? Arminian expositors see the inward gift followed by the outward sign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see baptism as the sign of what God has already done.

verses.text: He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.
verses.arminianNotes: He commands them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Arminian readers see the new believers welcomed into the church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a household baptism, which paedobaptists cite alongside 16:15 and 16:33.
